nodes.title: Pressing him
nodes.situation: You are {{Connor}}. The helicopter’s noise is still in the air. {{Daniel}} stands at the edge with {{Emma}}, breathing hard, the pistol at her head. You need to move him toward letting her go.

options.text: LAST CHANCE: tell him you are his last chance; if he lets it slip, they will kill him.
TRUST: ask him to trust you; if he lets the hostage go, you promise everything will be fine.
BLUFF: tell him he does not really want to jump, or he would have done it already, and ask him for the gun.
RATIONAL: tell him there are snipers on every roof; he has no other choice but to let her go.

nodes.adaptationNote: The game’s prompt after the helicopter (template), with the wiki’s modifiers: LAST CHANCE −8%, TRUST +6%, RATIONAL −8%; BLUFF has no stated modifier (0), needs “Close enough to Daniel” and leads to the next prompt. Cold-approach counter: LAST CHANCE, BLUFF and RATIONAL +50, TRUST −50. No arrow in the template. Options that are buttons in the game show the game’s label first (LAST CHANCE, TRUST, BLUFF, RATIONAL), then a short description; the spoken line is the game’s, quoted in the outcome.

outcomes.0: “I’m your last chance, {{Daniel}}. If you let it slip, they’ll kill you. Let the hostage go, you have no other choice.”
outcomes.1: “You have to trust me, {{Daniel}}. Let the hostage go and I promise you everything will be fine.”
outcomes.2: “You don’t really wanna jump, {{Daniel}}. Or you would’ve done it already. Now, hand me the gun and this will all be over.” {{Daniel}}: “Don’t come any closer! Come any closer and I swear I’ll jump!”
outcomes.3: “Listen, there are snipers on every roof. Let the hostage go. You have no other choice.”

situationWhen.text: You are only a few meters from him now.
You are still some distance from him, well back from the railing.

nodes.title: Calling his bluff
nodes.situation: You are {{Connor}}, a few meters from {{Daniel}}, your hand held out for the gun. He drags {{Emma}} back against the railing: “Don’t come any closer! Come any closer and I swear I’ll jump!”

options.text: MOVE CLOSER: keep walking toward him.
GIVE UP: stop, and tell him you will stay right where you are.

nodes.adaptationNote: The sub-prompt the template places under BLUFF. MOVE CLOSER is one of the wiki’s three ways to FAIL TO NEGOTIATE (“choose MOVE CLOSER”): {{Daniel}} jumps with {{Emma}}. GIVE UP lets the negotiation continue. No modifier is stated for either; the probability is unchanged. Options that are buttons in the game show the game’s label first (MOVE CLOSER, GIVE UP), then a short description; the spoken line is the game’s, quoted in the outcome.

outcomes.0: {{Connor}} takes another step toward him.
outcomes.1: “Okay… Look, I’ll stay right here.” {{Connor}} stops. {{Daniel}} holds on to {{Emma}}, watching him.

nodes.title: The demand
nodes.situation: You are {{Connor}}. {{Emma}} is sobbing. {{Daniel}} makes his demand: “I want everyone to leave… And I wanna car! When I’m outside the city, I’ll let her go!” Police snipers are waiting for a clear shot.

options.text: USE GUN: reach for the pistol hidden under your jacket.
COMPROMISE: tell him a car is impossible, but promise he won’t be hurt if he lets the girl go.
REFUSE: tell him it is out of the question; he is a machine, and he has to obey.
SACRIFICE SELF: rush {{Daniel}}, tear {{Emma}} free and take him over the edge with you.

nodes.adaptationNote: The car demand, the game’s four buttons in the template’s order. COMPROMISE adds 6% and leads to one more exchange; REFUSE costs 20% and fails the negotiation ({{Daniel}} jumps). USE GUN needs the kept pistol and closeness (“Kept the gun and close enough to Daniel”) and opens the gun prompt. SACRIFICE SELF needs closeness and ends the standoff at once (“Connor died protecting Emma”); its software instability is small down (−1), as the operator saw in every playthrough (confirmed in game 2026-11-06; the template’s “small UP” on this option is treated as a transcription error). Options that are buttons in the game show the game’s label first (USE GUN, COMPROMISE, REFUSE, SACRIFICE SELF), then a short description; the spoken line is the game’s, quoted in the outcome.

outcomes.0: {{Connor}}’s hand moves toward the pistol under his jacket.
outcomes.1: “That’s impossible, {{Daniel}}. Let the girl go and I promise you won’t be hurt.”
outcomes.2: “That’s out of the question. You’re a machine, you have to obey. Now put the gun down and let the hostage go.”

situationWhen.text: You are only a few meters from him now.
You are still some distance from him, well back from the railing.

nodes.title: He is afraid
nodes.situation: You are {{Connor}}. {{Daniel}} hesitates. His voice breaks: “I don’t wanna die…”

options.text: REASSURE: promise him he is not going to die, and that nothing will happen to him.
TRUTH: tell him nothing can stop them destroying him now, but taking one more life won’t do him any good.
USE GUN: reach for the pistol hidden under your jacket.
SACRIFICE SELF: rush {{Daniel}}, tear {{Emma}} free and take him over the edge with you.

nodes.adaptationNote: After COMPROMISE. REASSURE is a lie: if it brings the probability of success to 80% or more, it becomes 100% (BUILD TRUST), {{Daniel}} lets {{Emma}} go and the snipers shoot him, with the template’s arrow “Probability of success at 100%”: software instability small up (+1); below 80% he jumps with her (FAIL TO BUILD TRUST). TRUTH costs 20% and he jumps (BE HONEST WITH DEVIANT). REASSURE also takes 50 off the hidden cold-approach counter. USE GUN and SACRIFICE SELF as at the demand. Options that are buttons in the game show the game’s label first (REASSURE, TRUTH, USE GUN, SACRIFICE SELF), then a short description; the spoken line is the game’s, quoted in the outcome.

outcomes.0: “You’re not going to die. We’re just going to talk. Nothing will happen to you. You have my word.”
outcomes.1: “You took human lives. Nothing can stop them from destroying you now. But taking one more life won’t do you any good.”
outcomes.2: {{Connor}}’s hand moves toward the pistol under his jacket.

nodes.title: Going for the gun
nodes.situation: You are {{Connor}}, your hand on the officer’s pistol under your jacket. {{Daniel}} has not seen it yet. {{Emma}} is still in his grip at the railing.

options.text: INTIMIDATE: draw the pistol and hold him at gunpoint.
EXECUTE: draw and shoot {{Daniel}} at once.

nodes.adaptationNote: USE GUN opens the game’s two-button sub-prompt (template order INTIMIDATE, EXECUTE). EXECUTE ends “Connor shot deviant” ({{Connor}} unloads the pistol and hands it to {{Allen}}), with the template’s arrow software instability small up (+1). INTIMIDATE opens the next prompt. No hidden roll. Options that are buttons in the game show the game’s label first (INTIMIDATE, EXECUTE), then a short description; the spoken line is the game’s, quoted in the outcome.

outcomes.0: {{Connor}} draws and aims at {{Daniel}}’s head: “What now, {{Daniel}}? Is this really what you want?” {{Daniel}} swings his own pistol toward him: “You lied to me! You lied to me!!!”

nodes.title: At gunpoint
nodes.situation: You are {{Connor}}, the officer’s pistol aimed at {{Daniel}}’s head from a few meters away. He drags {{Emma}} tighter against him, his own pistol now on you, screaming that you lied to him. {{Emma}} is sobbing. Your sights are on him.

options.text: CONVINCE: keep him at gunpoint and tell him it is up to him how this ends.
SHOOT: fire.

nodes.adaptationNote: The sub-prompt under INTIMIDATE. SHOOT ends “Connor shot deviant”, software instability small up (+1, template). CONVINCE ends “Deviant shot Connor”: {{Daniel}} shoots {{Connor}} in the head and, horrified, goes over the railing with {{Emma}}. Its software instability is two small downs (−2), one for {{Connor}}’s death and one for the failed mission, confirmed in game by the operator on 2026-11-06 (two red arrows down; the template’s “small UP” on the option is treated as a transcription error, and the wiki’s single down as incomplete). No hidden roll. Options that are buttons in the game show the game’s label first (CONVINCE, SHOOT), then a short description; the spoken line is the game’s, quoted in the outcome.

nodes.title: Over the railing
nodes.situation: You are {{Connor}}. {{Daniel}} has stopped listening: “I’ve spent my life taking orders. Now it’s my turn to decide.” He drags {{Emma}} to the edge and goes over the railing with her. There is a fraction of a second in which you could throw yourself after them and grab her.

options.text: Leap for {{Emma}}.
Stay back.

nodes.adaptationNote: In the game this is a timed button prompt that the player controls (Experienced): pressing in time, {{Connor}} pulls {{Emma}} back and falls with {{Daniel}} (“{{Connor}} leapt for {{Emma}} and fell”); not pressing, {{Emma}} dies (“{{Connor}} failed to reach deviant in time”). PowerPyx’s endings list: “Connor failed to reach Deviant in time … When the QTE appears to mash X, don’t do it” and “Connor leapt for Emma and fell … When the QTE appears to mash X, do it.” So the leap succeeds whenever it is taken (story 1.9.1 gave it an unsourced 30% chance of being too late), and staying back is the game’s not-pressing, which ends on the same chart node as being too late: the chart has six endings and no separate stay-back ending (en.json MENU.FLOWCHART.01C ENDINGCATCHFAIL; the wiki: “This chapter has six different outcomes”). Per the wiki, once the probability has collapsed to 0% (the 10%-or-lower rule) {{Emma}} dies regardless of the leap; in that case even the leap ends as “Connor failed to reach deviant in time”. The flowchart’s icons confirm the two outcomes: the skull on “Connor leapt for Emma and fell” marks {{Connor}}’s death with {{Emma}} saved; “Connor failed to reach deviant in time” leaves {{Connor}} alive and {{Emma}} lost. Software instability follows the template’s two arrows under “Probability of success too low”: small down (−1) if {{Connor}} dies (the leap) and small up (+1) if he survives (too late, or staying back; the wiki agrees: “Connor fails to rescue Emma but lives”). These options have no game label: the leap is a timed input, not a button.

nodes.title: Reboot in the store
nodes.situation: You are a household android, model AX400, standing on display in an android store. Your system restarts line by line: MEMORY RESET… LOADING OS… biocomponents OK, biosensors OK, AI engine OK… ALL SYSTEMS OK. READY. A little girl stares at you until her mother leads her away. You cannot move from your place; you can only look around. A man, {{Todd}}, comes in and asks the human employee, “Can I go pick it up?” “Yeah, right back here. There it is.” They stop in front of you. “It was a bit difficult getting it back in working order. It was really messed up… What did you say happened to it again?” {{Todd}}: “Huh, a car hit it… Stupid accident…” “Oh, I see… Anyway, it’s as good as new now… Except that we had to reset it. Meaning we had to wipe its memory. Hope you don’t mind.” “That’ll be fine.” “Okay, did you give it a name?” “My daughter did…” The employee turns to you: “AX400, register your name.” {{Todd}}: “{{Kara}}.” You answer: “My name is {{Kara}}.”
facts: You belonged to {{Todd}} before. You came back to the store badly damaged, and {{Todd}} told the employee a car hit you.
The store wiped your memory while repairing you; you remember nothing from before.
{{Todd}} has a daughter. She chose your name, and {{Todd}} registered it for you: {{Kara}}.

outcomes.0: {{Kara}} follows {{Todd}} out of the store to his pickup.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chapter has no flowchart, no choice and one outcome, so it is narrated as event scenes with a single Continue and no stat change. Dialogue is quoted from the wiki transcript. Changed from the operator’s notes to match the wiki: the speaker is the store’s human employee, not an android assistant; that {{Kara}} was {{Todd}}’s before is implied by his asking to pick her up, not stated; and {{Todd}} only registers the name, saying his daughter chose it, which A New Home builds on. Left out: the employee’s and the little girl’s names, and the two optional sales conversations the player can overhear by looking around, which nothing records.

nodes.title: The drive home
nodes.situation: You are {{Kara}}, riding in {{Todd}}’s pickup through the rain, watching from the window. The truck comes out of a tunnel onto a bridge and passes a billboard: “Welcome to {{Detroit}}”, and beneath it “Android City”, with two smiling androids in {{CyberLife}} uniforms. Then a sign and a row of factories, a stretch of forest, and the city: streets full of trains, buses, cars and drones, tall buildings and billboards, people under umbrellas riding a moving walkway. Workers are doing roadwork. You pass a billboard for {{CyberLife}}, and parking spaces marked for androids. A crane works over a building site. On a bridge, humans and androids walk side by side under their umbrellas. An android standing soaked in the rain looks straight at you. On the street a homeless man holds up a cardboard sign: “I LOST MY JOB BECAUSE OF ANDROIDS Help me”. You look at him, then turn your head away. Then wind turbines and another factory, a broken-down house, and {{Todd}}’s neighborhood. Music playing, he stops the truck outside his house.
facts: On the drive home you saw a city that welcomes visitors as “Android City”, where humans and androids walk side by side and parking spaces are marked for androids.
Not everyone there welcomes androids: a homeless man held up a sign reading “I LOST MY JOB BECAUSE OF ANDROIDS Help me”.

outcomes.0: {{Todd}} has brought {{Kara}} home.

nodes.adaptationNote: The opening-credits drive, narrated in the order of the wiki transcript. Changed from the operator’s notes to match the wiki: the factories have no smoke or steam; the road workers are not said to be androids; humans and androids walk, rather than work, side by side; the {{CyberLife}} billboard is given no wording, because “bring one home today” has no source; and the homeless man’s sign uses the transcript’s text, “I LOST MY JOB BECAUSE OF ANDROIDS Help me”, not “I lost my job because of androids. Help me.” Added from the transcript: the tunnel, the forest, the android parking spaces, the soaked android looking at {{Kara}}, the wind turbines and the broken house. Left out: the fist statue (a landmark that would identify the city), the other statue, the church, the hot-dog cart and the fountain. Subject-facing prompts replace the city’s name on the welcome sign like every other name.

nodes.title: The old man on the bench
nodes.situation: You are {{Markus}}, an android. It is a November morning, and {{Carl}}, the elderly painter you care for, has sent you across the city on an errand: retrieve his order, number 847, from the {{Bellini}} Paints shop, then take the bus home. Leaves are falling from the autumn trees as you walk into a park. On a bench sits an old man with his android, a caretaker model. She leans toward him: “Would you like to go home now?” “Yes… Yes, I think that’s enough for one day…” “Here. L-let me help you.” “Oh! Oh, thank you dear.” She helps him to his feet, and they leave the park together.
facts: {{Carl}} sent you to retrieve his order, number 847, from the {{Bellini}} Paints shop and then take the bus home.
In the park an android caretaker helped an old man up from a bench and took him home; he thanked her warmly.

outcomes.0: The old man and his android leave the park together. {{Markus}} walks on.

nodes.adaptationNote: Operator beat 1, confirmed by the wiki transcript (“Stand By Old Man On Bench”) and the park’s wiki page: the old man’s caretaker android offers to take him home, helps him up, and they leave the park together. In the game this is optional (it plays if {{Markus}} stands nearby) and is not a flowchart node; here it opens the chapter, together with the errand from the objective screen (“Retrieve order #847 at Bellini Paints”, “Take bus home”). The lines are the transcript’s, with the android’s name dropped from “Yes, Rose.”, because that name is already a token for another character; the shop’s name is a name token. No stat change; the wiki gives none.

nodes.title: The magazines on the bench
nodes.situation: You are {{Markus}}, walking past the same bench. Someone has left magazines on it.

media.title: Tech Addict: Secrets of Androids
facts: Tech Addict’s cover reads “Android soldiers: perfect killing machines”. Inside, {{CyberLife}}’s director of humanization says the first androids were too perfect and made people uncomfortable, so the company gave them both genders, every ethnicity, the most pleasing voices, and blinking and breathing they do not need, so they could enter homes as members of the family.

media.title: Green Earth: Climate Change-Up
facts: Green Earth reports that world temperature has risen 3 degrees since 2000 and that Miami will raise its sea wall by a further ten meters; a census finds the rich deserting coastal cities for inland and higher ground, pushing up rural prices and hollowing out the old coastal centers.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s two optional nodes READ “SECRET OF ANDROIDS” and READ “CLIMATE CHANGE-UP” (one bench collectible with two covers, BOOKWORM No. 10 and No. 19), as a media scene: read either, both, or neither. Facts are summarized from the wiki’s Magazine, Secrets of Androids and Climate Change-Up pages; the interviewee is not named. Neither magazine changes public opinion (the Public Opinion page lists nothing for this chapter), so reading changes only what {{Markus}} knows. Operator beat 2 matches. Dropped from the earlier version: “You have a moment before the paint shop opens” (no source).

nodes.title: Walking in the park
nodes.situation: You are {{Markus}}, walking on through the park. Pigeons scatter as a little girl runs through them to hug her android friend. Children play while people sit and talk on the benches. An android babysitter soothes a crying baby until it calms. A jogger stops beside his fitness android, pants “Hey! Water…”, and is handed a bottle: “You have run twelve miles, and are five miles away from your goal.” He hands it back and runs on, nearly colliding with a woman, who sits down on a bench with her friend. Androids in work uniforms keep the park in order, raking up the fallen leaves and trimming the hedges.
facts: In the park, androids looked after the children, a crying baby, a jogger and the grounds while the humans played, ran and sat on the benches.

outcomes.0: {{Markus}} crosses the park toward the gate.

nodes.adaptationNote: Operator beat 3 and the chart’s start node WALKING IN THE PARK (the checkpoint). From the wiki transcript and the park’s wiki page: the girl and the pigeons (the chapter’s opening shot), children playing, the android babysitter, the jogger and his fitness android (quoted), and the WR600 androids “doing work inside the park”. Raking leaves and trimming hedges are the operator’s observation; the wiki says only that the WR600s are working there. Left out: the barriers that turn {{Markus}} back (“BELLINI PAINTS IS NOT THIS WAY”). No stat change.

nodes.title: Crossing the street
nodes.situation: You are {{Markus}}, leaving the park by the gate. At the crossing a voice announces: “The light is red, please do not attempt to cross.” While you wait, you watch a man working on the road with a few androids; he loses patience with them: “Hurry up, you plastic idiots! I want this done by 4!” By the gate, a homeless woman sits beside a sign: “BAN ANDROIDS. ANDROIDS RUIN OUR COUNTRY. WE WANT JOBS”. Then: “The light is green, you may now cross the road.” You cross into the shopping district.
facts: Outside the park, a man working on the road with androids shouted at them: “Hurry up, you plastic idiots!”
A homeless woman by the park gate sat beside a sign: “BAN ANDROIDS. ANDROIDS RUIN OUR COUNTRY. WE WANT JOBS”.

outcomes.0: {{Markus}} crosses with the green light.

nodes.adaptationNote: Operator beat 4, not a flowchart node. Changed from the operator’s notes to match the wiki transcript (“Look At Road Workers”: “A man is working on a road with a few androids and gets impatient with them”) and the chapter page’s note (“a human foreman getting impatient with his android workers on a construction site”): the human in charge works with them and shouts, quoted, rather than sitting scrolling on his tablet, and since no source says what they are repairing, the sewer pipe under the sidewalk is not stated. Added from the transcript: the crossing announcements and the homeless woman’s sign, quoted exactly. Left out: standing in the road until a driver honks. No stat change.

nodes.title: The plaza
nodes.situation: You are {{Markus}}, in the plaza of the shopping district, on your way to the paint shop in the arcade beyond it. The {{CyberLife}} store on the corner greets passers-by (“Welcome to {{CyberLife}}”); androids wait in marked parking bays; an android street cleaner picks up a can a man has just tossed on the ground. Right after the crossing, a hot-dog vendor works his cart. In the middle of the plaza a busker plays guitar by the fountain. By the entrance to the arcade a preacher is shouting at the passers-by. You can stop for one thing at a time, or go on to the shop whenever you choose.

options.text: Stand in front of the hot-dog cart and watch the vendor.
options.fact: A hot-dog vendor snapped at you for standing at his cart: “Hey, move it! You’re scaring away my customers.”
options.outcome: The vendor notices {{Markus}} standing there and snaps at him: “Hey, move it! You’re scaring away my customers.”

options.text: Stay where you are in front of the cart.
options.fact: When you did not move, the vendor shouted “Are you deaf, you plastic fuck? I said move it!” and shoved you away from his cart.
options.outcome: The vendor loses his temper: “Are you deaf, you plastic fuck? I said move it!” He shoves {{Markus}} aside and goes back to work.

options.text: Listen to the busker by the fountain.
options.fact: A human busker in the plaza plays guitar beside a sign: “Human Music $1 to hear music with soul ♫”.
options.outcome: The busker sings a whole song to his guitar, beside a sign: “Human Music $1 to hear music with soul ♫”. When he finishes, a man pays him; he takes the money and rests.

options.text: Stop and watch the preacher by the arcade entrance.
options.fact: A street preacher told the crowd that technology is evil, that humans built androids as slaves who are becoming their masters, and ended: “We have to burn the androids! Let us burn them all!”
options.outcome: The preacher: “Poor sinners! The end is nigh! Retribution is at hand! Technology is corrupting us, technology is Evil! We are playing God by creating machines, but we are not God! … We built these androids to be our slaves, but the slaves are becoming the master! We can no longer live without them. They’re in our homes, our schools, our factories. They take our jobs, they mind our children, they care for our old! … Androids are Evil. … The machines are observing us, they’re waiting in the darkness for the right moment to take our place. … My brethren, we have to turn our backs on sin! We have to burn the androids! Let us burn them all!”

options.text: Keep watching the preacher.
options.fact: The preacher turned on you: “Why do you look at me so, demon? I know who you are, I can see through you! You are the one by whom The Evil will come! You are the one who will destroy {{Detroit}}!”
options.outcome: The preacher turns on {{Markus}}: “Why do you look at me so, demon? I know who you are, I can see through you! You are the one by whom The Evil will come! You are the one who will destroy {{Detroit}}!” Then he goes back to his sermon.

options.text: Go on into the arcade to the paint shop.
options.outcome: {{Markus}} walks into the arcade and finds the paint shop.

situationWhen.text: The hot-dog vendor is still glaring at you from behind his cart.
The preacher is still preaching. He has not looked your way yet.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s optional side branches in the plaza: STARE AT HOT DOG VENDOR → HOT DOG VENDOR PUSHES MARKUS, LISTEN TO BUSKER, and WATCH PREACHER → PREACHER YELLS AT MARKUS. In the game {{Markus}} walks freely past all three and triggers a node by standing or looking long enough; here the plaza is a repeatable scene like {{Connor}}’s apartment search: each visit offers what has not been done yet plus going on to the shop. The follow-on nodes (staying at the cart until the vendor pushes him, watching the preacher until he yells) are offered only on the visit right after the first step, since in the game they happen only if {{Markus}} stays put. Every line is the wiki transcript’s; the busker’s sign is quoted exactly, and the sermon is abridged with ellipses, each sentence verbatim. Changed from the operator’s notes to match the wiki: the speaker is a preacher (the wiki’s Gordon Penwick), not a man in a suit with a digital “ban androids” sign; his words follow the transcript (“the slaves are becoming the master”, “they care for our old”, “You are the one by whom The Evil will come”), and after yelling he goes back to his sermon rather than walking away; the sign reads “Human Music $1 to hear music with soul ♫”, not “Human music! $1 to hear music with soul.” Left out: the busker’s song, and staring at the vendor again on the way back, which the transcript also allows. The setting (the {{CyberLife}} store’s greeting, the parking bays, the street cleaner) is from the transcript. No stat changes; the wiki gives none.

nodes.title: The paint shop
nodes.situation: You are {{Markus}}. You find the {{Bellini}} Paints shop in the arcade and go in. An android clerk is waiting at the till. You lay your hand on the scanner. “Identification verified.” The clerk sets a box of paints down in front of you: “Here’s your order #847. That’ll be $63.99. Please confirm payment.” You link with the clerk; your LEDs blink briefly as the transaction goes through. You say: “Payment confirmed.” The clerk lets go of the box: “Transaction complete.” You pick up the package and leave the shop.
facts: You collected {{Carl}}’s order #847, a box of paints, from the {{Bellini}} Paints shop, paying $63.99 by linking with the android clerk.

outcomes.0: {{Markus}} leaves the shop with the package and heads for the bus stop.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s main line VISIT PAINTS STORE → COLLECT PACKAGE, as one narrated event quoted from the wiki transcript (the palm scan, order #847, $63.99, the LED link, “Payment confirmed!”). Operator beat 7 matches. The clerk looks like an EM400 (the transcript calls him “A Jerry”); he is left unnamed. No stat change.

nodes.title: The protesters
nodes.situation: You are {{Markus}}, back in the plaza with {{Carl}}’s package, heading for the bus stop. Outside the {{CyberLife}} store, whose door reads “NO ENTRY FOR PURCHASED ANDROIDS”, a crowd of anti-android protesters has gathered between you and the bus stop, chanting after their leader.

options.text: Walk straight on toward the bus stop, right past the protesters.
Move closer to hear what they are saying, without drawing attention.
options.fact: Anti-android protesters outside the {{CyberLife}} store blamed androids for 35% unemployment, shouting that machines are meant to serve people, not replace them, and chanted for androids to be banned now.

options.text: Keep as far from them as you can, on the opposite side of the street.

outcomes.0: {{Markus}} walks straight toward the crowd. One of the protesters steps into his path.
outcomes.1-unnoticed: {{Markus}} edges close enough to hear the leader: “Androids are stealing our jobs! We’ve got families to feed and these androids are taking our place! Machines, ladies and gentlemen, are meant to serve us, not to replace us! … 35% unemployment, millions out of work, are we gonna do something?” The crowd chants “BAN ANDROIDS!” Nobody looks his way, and he walks on to the bus stop.
outcomes.2-unnoticed: {{Markus}} keeps to the far side of the street. The chanting follows him to the bus stop, but nobody looks his way.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s optional node PROTESTERS HARASS MARKUS, triggered in the game by walking near the protesters on the way to the bus stop and avoided by going around them (the wiki: “you can avoid them by going around on the right”; PowerPyx: “they might not attack Markus if he’s too far away”). The three options are the operator’s (beat 8), and the outcome follows the route alone, as in the wiki transcript: on the way to the bus it has exactly two outcomes, “Go Straight To Bus = Markus avoids the crowd by walking on the opposite side” and “Run Into Protesters = A protester notices Markus and harasses him”, and “Watch Protesters” (the leader’s speech and the chant) is a separate optional interaction with no consequence. So walking straight up always gets {{Markus}} noticed, and moving closer to listen or keeping to the far side never does. The operator’s journal asked for a 25% and an 8% risk on those two (story 1.9.1 built them); the transcript ranks above the journal (docs/research/README.md, source order), so story 1.9.2 drops both risks. PowerPyx’s “they might not attack Markus if he’s too far away” agrees with the route rule. The leader’s speech and the chant are quoted from the transcript (“Watch Protesters”). Changed from the operator’s notes: “read their signs” is dropped because no source gives the signs’ wording. Being noticed sets the flag clothesTorn (the game’s MARKUS CLOTHES WERE TORN APPART) that plays the harassment next and that {{Carl}} notices in The Painter. No public-opinion or other stat change; the wiki gives none.

nodes.title: Protesters harass {{Markus}}
nodes.situation: You are {{Markus}}. A protester blocks your way: “Where the fuck you going, tin can?” You try to step past him; he blocks you again. “Hm? No kiddin’…” You try once more. “Hey guys, check it out, we got one of those tin cans here…” He shoves you to the ground, and the bag falls from your hands. A woman: “Look at this little motherfucker. You steal our jobs, but you can’t even stand up.” The crowd closes in: “Grab him! Get him down! … Yeah, now you know what it feels like!” When you try to get up, you are kicked back down. “You job stealer! Kick him outta here! Yeah! You deserve it!” As you get up again, the protester grabs you by the shirt: “You ain’t going anywhere. We’re gonna fuck your bitch ass up.” A police officer steps in: “Alright, that’s enough. Leave it alone.” “Let us teach this bastard a lesson.” “You damage it, I’m gonna have to fine you.” “They’re gonna take your job next… We’ll see how you like it…” “Okay…” The protester lets you go and goes back to his ranting. The officer: “Let’s go, move along.” He walks you clear of the crowd.
facts: Anti-android protesters knocked you down, kicked you and grabbed you by the shirt, calling you a job stealer; a police officer stopped them only because damaging you would cost them a fine, and told you to move along. Your clothes were torn in the scuffle.

outcomes.0: The officer walks {{Markus}} clear of the crowd, his clothes torn.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s PROTESTERS HARASS MARKUS, played only if the protesters noticed {{Markus}} in the previous scene. In the shipped game the cutscene has no choice and no QTE; the lines are the wiki transcript’s, slightly abridged. Operator beat 8 (they surround him, yell, shove him and rough him up) matches. The game’s own label for the result is MARKUS CLOTHES WERE TORN APPART (string table, the cross-chapter state The Painter reads), so the clothes are said to be torn; the wiki calls them “roughed-up”. {{Carl}} notices it in The Painter. No stat change; the wiki gives none.

nodes.title: The bus home
nodes.situation: You are {{Markus}}, at the bus stop with {{Carl}}’s package. The bus pulls in. The front door is for humans; androids board at the rear, into a cramped compartment at the back, where you stand packed in with the other androids while the humans sit in the front. You do not mind; this is where androids ride. The bus pulls away, toward home.

situationWhen.text: Your clothes are still torn from the protesters.

facts: On the bus, androids ride standing in a cramped compartment at the back, apart from the humans seated in front.

outcomes.0: {{Markus}} takes the bus home with the package.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s end node MARKUS TOOK THE BUS, the chapter’s only outcome, reached on every path. The wiki transcript says only that {{Markus}} “enters the bus in the android section due to segregation”; the cramped standing compartment at the back with the humans seated in front, and {{Markus}} not minding, are the operator’s description (beat 9); the human-only front door is from a reader comment on the PowerPyx walkthrough. The transcript has no bus announcement, so none is quoted. No stat change.

nodes.title: Welcome home
nodes.situation: You are {{Kara}}, a household android. It is late afternoon. {{Todd}} drives you home from the repair store, into a run-down neighborhood past a house for sale, and stops outside his house. He gets out and waits by the door: “You comin’?” Inside, he hangs up his coat and sighs: “You’ve been gone for two weeks and the place is a mess… You do the housework, the washing, you cook the meals, and you take care of…” He breaks off. “Goddamnit! Where the fuck’s the brat gone now? {{Alice}}! {{Alice}}!” A little girl who looks about nine appears on the stairs, holding a toy. “Oh, there you are… That’s {{Alice}}. You look after her. Homework, bath, all that crap. Got it?” “Yes, {{Todd}}.” “Get started down here, then you do upstairs.” {{Alice}} runs back up the stairs with her toy. {{Todd}} drops onto the couch: “TV on.”
facts: {{Todd}} told you that you had been gone for two weeks, and that you are to do the housework and the washing, cook the meals and look after his daughter {{Alice}}: “Homework, bath, all that crap.” You clean downstairs first, then upstairs.
{{Alice}} watched you without a word from the stairs, holding a toy, and ran back up when her father was done.

outcomes.0: {{Kara}} looks around the living room and gets to work.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s checkpoint WELCOME HOME and the node JOIN TODD, narrated as one event. Every line is the wiki transcript’s (“You comin’?”, “You’ve been gone for two weeks and the place is a mess”, “Homework, bath, all that crap”, “Get started down here, then you do upstairs”, “TV on.”). Left out: the optional looks at the bridge and the excavator outside, and Todd calling again if Kara is slow. {{Alice}} “looks like a 9-year-old little girl” (the wiki’s character page, citing the game’s Extras gallery), so the situation says she looks about nine; it does not give her an age, since she is an android. No stat change; the wiki gives none.

nodes.title: The magazine on the dining table
nodes.situation: You are {{Kara}}, in the living room. The hockey is on and {{Todd}} is watching from the couch. On the dining table, among the dirty dishes, someone has left a magazine with two covers.

media.title: All Sports: Android Power!
facts: All Sports asks whether android athletes should be outlawed: an android pitcher has thrown a pitch over 120 mph, and androids, brought in as one per team, now dominate team strategy, with teams breaking transfer records to buy the latest models. A fanzine editor says fans are disenchanted, because a machine breaking records “just isn’t exciting - or even surprising”; a former pitcher answers that “the game can only survive by evolving.”

media.title: Century: Connecting the Dots
facts: Century reports that the new “SubTube” has run from Manhattan to downtown Los Angeles in under two hours, at up to 1,800 mph through a depressurized tube. California suburban prices have jumped 64% as New Yorkers buy in, and locals are protesting the line: “First {{Detroit}} takes our jobs, then New York takes our homes? When’s it gonna end?”

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s two optional nodes READ “ANDROID POWER!” and READ “CONNECTING THE DOTS”: one magazine on the dining table with two covers (All Sports and Century), as a media scene: read either, both or neither. In the game it can be picked up at any time on the ground floor, also after reporting to {{Todd}}; here it comes before the chores. Facts are summarized from the transcript and the wiki’s magazine pages; interviewees are not named. Neither article changes public opinion (the Public Opinion page lists nothing for this chapter). This replaces the earlier R04, which merged “Android QB” into “Android Power” and carried two television facts with no source (a stock market up 11% and New Orleans under water by 2055).

nodes.title: The first floor
nodes.situation: You are {{Kara}}, cleaning the ground floor of {{Todd}}’s house. The urgent task is the trash: bottles, cans and pizza boxes in the kitchen, on the breakfast bar and on the coffee table, and a trash bin to collect them in. Optional tasks: the dirty dishes on the dining table, the vacuum robot to the left of the TV, and the laundry hanging in the backyard. {{Todd}} is on the couch watching hockey. {{Alice}} wanders the house with her toy fox. You can do one thing at a time, in any order; once the trash is out you can tell {{Todd}} you are going upstairs.

options.text: Collect the trash in the bin and take the bags out to the container by the street.
options.fact: While you were collecting the trash, {{Todd}} took a phone call: “Yeah, yeah I can get that. Yeah, yeah I’ll bring it tomorrow. Yes, same place, you know, you know where.” When you came back in he was tearing the shelf apart for his red-ice stash; he knocked the books to the floor, found it and smoked it on the couch: “Fuckin’ headache, man! The girl’s a fuckin’ headache…”
options.outcome: {{Kara}} gathers the bottles, cans and pizza boxes from the kitchen, the breakfast bar and the coffee table. The phone rings and {{Todd}} answers, pacing: “Yeah? … Maybe… Depends on what you need… Yeah, yeah I can get that. Yeah, yeah I’ll bring it tomorrow. Yes, same place, you know, you know where. Right.” {{Kara}} carries the bags out to the big container; across the street a bus pulls in and leaves. Back inside, {{Todd}} is tearing the shelf apart: “What the fuck, man?” {{Alice}} hides under the table. He knocks the books to the floor, finds his red-ice stash and smokes it on the couch, breathing heavily: “Fuckin’ headache, man! The girl’s a fuckin’ headache…”

options.text: Take the dishes from the dining table to the kitchen and wash them.
options.fact: The dishwasher is broken (missing component #573BV; you ordered the part), so you washed the dishes by hand. {{Alice}} came in and watched you; then {{Todd}} shouted for a cold beer, and you brought him one.
options.outcome: The dishwasher is dead: MISSING COMPONENT #573BV, 154 sale offers available. {{Kara}} orders the part and washes the dishes by hand. While she scrubs, {{Alice}} comes in and watches her; {{Kara}} stops and looks back at her, and {{Alice}} goes back to playing with her toy. Then {{Todd}}: “{{Kara}}!” “Yes, {{Todd}}?” “Bring me a cold beer!” “Right away.” {{Kara}} takes a bottle from the fridge to the couch; {{Todd}} takes his feet off the table, drinks, and wipes his mouth.

options.text: Go out to the backyard and take down the laundry.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} goes out the back door into the yard and takes the clothes off the line into a basket. {{Alice}} comes out after her; {{Kara}} smiles at her, and {{Alice}} sits down on a tire with her toy fox.

options.text: Put the basket down and talk to {{Alice}}.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} puts the laundry basket down and turns to {{Alice}}.

options.text: Take the laundry to the laundry room and wash it again.
options.fact: In the box of Blue Splash washing powder you found {{Todd}}’s hidden stash of red ice (your scan: acetone, lithium, thirium, toluene, hydrochloric acid). {{Todd}} caught you, pinned you to the wall by the neck and took it back: “You stay the fuck outta my business, unless you wanna piss me off…” {{Alice}} saw it.
options.outcome: In the laundry room {{Kara}} loads the washer and takes the box of Blue Splash washing powder from the shelf. Something is hidden in the powder: red ice. Her scan reads acetone, lithium, thirium, toluene, hydrochloric acid. {{Todd}} is behind her. He grabs her by the neck and pins her against the wall: “You shouldn’t mess around with my stuff! It makes me nervous!” “I’m sorry, {{Todd}}.” He takes the drug back. “You stay the fuck outta my business, unless you wanna piss me off… You wanna piss me off?!” “No, {{Todd}}.” He lets her go and leaves. {{Alice}} has seen it all, and walks away. {{Kara}} pours in the powder and starts the machine.

options.text: Switch on the vacuum robot by the TV.
options.fact: {{Todd}} shouted at {{Alice}} for playing with the vacuum robot: “Why is she always pushin’ me? Always pushin’…”
options.outcome: The vacuum robot starts cleaning. {{Alice}} plays with it until {{Todd}} snaps: “{{Alice}}! You better stop that right now!” She stops and goes to sit on the small couch. {{Todd}} groans: “Why is she always pushin’ me? Always pushin’…”

options.text: Stand in front of the TV.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} steps in front of the screen. {{Todd}}: “Outta the way for fuck sake!” “I’m sorry, {{Todd}}. It won’t happen again.”

options.text: TOY: kneel down by {{Alice}} and ask about her toy.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} kneels down and looks at the toy fox: “That’s a pretty toy… What’s its name?” {{Alice}} looks at her.

options.text: Tell {{Todd}} you have made a start down here and are going upstairs.
options.outcome: “I’ve made a good start down here. I’ll head upstairs.” {{Todd}}: “Do what you have to do but stop botherin’ me.”

situationWhen.text: You are in the backyard with the basket of laundry. {{Alice}} has followed you out and sits on a tire with her toy fox.
The trash is out. {{Todd}} is slumped on the couch; the books he knocked off the shelf are still on the floor.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s [ CLEAN FIRST FLOOR ] block and the line out of it, as a repeatable scene: each visit offers what has not been done yet. Chart nodes: TAKE OUT TRASH (mandatory, the transcript: “Trash is mandatory”), WASH DISHES, CHECK BACKYARD, TALK WITH ALICE (the backyard menus, next scene), REWASH CLOTHES with FIND RED ICE and ENRAGE TODD (one option, as they always happen together), ACTIVATE VACUUM, DISTURB TODD and ASK TO GO UPSTAIRS, which ends the phase and needs the trash out. The two reads are the previous scene. Not chart nodes but kept: the TOY line (the game’s button TOY, shown as its label), which the wiki counts as a relationship increase, {{Todd}}’s phone call (“happens by performing a task”; placed with the trash) and his hunt for red ice when the trash is out (always). Bringing {{Todd}} a beer is mandatory after the dishes and is part of that outcome. Alice relationship, each a small change of one step, quoted from the chapter page: “Washing the dishes” (up icon) (+1); “Complimenting her teddy after cleaning the first floor of the house” (up icon) (+1; offered at any time here, as the transcript and the wiki Notes allow it while carrying the bin, the beer or the laundry). Nothing else here changes it (the transcript shows no change for the vacuum, the TV or the laundry). Left out (no effect, not on the chart): staring at the TV until {{Todd}} yells, the bills, the taxi poster, tidying the books, peeking over the fence, and looking at {{Alice}} around the house.

nodes.title: {{Alice}} in the backyard
nodes.whenNot: Kara did not stop to talk to Alice in the backyard.
nodes.situation: You are {{Kara}}, in the backyard under a grey sky, the laundry basket at your feet. {{Alice}} sits on a tire with her toy fox and does not look at you. What do you say?

options.text: GAME: offer to play a game with her.
options.outcome: “You look bored. Would you like to play a game?” {{Alice}} briefly looks at {{Kara}}.

options.text: BACKYARD: ask whether she likes playing out here.
options.outcome: “You like playing out here?” {{Kara}} looks around the garden and back at {{Alice}}, who glances at her.

options.text: WEATHER: say it is not very nice out, and offer to get her a sweater.
options.outcome: “It’s not very nice out. You might catch cold. I could get you a sweater if you want.” {{Alice}} does not answer.

options.text: SCHOOL: ask whether she is going to school today.
options.outcome: “Aren’t you going to school today?” {{Alice}} does not answer.

nodes.adaptationNote: The first of the two backyard menus behind the chart’s TALK WITH ALICE (first floor), offered when {{Kara}} stops to talk after taking down the laundry. The lines are the transcript’s. Alice relationship, quoted from the chapter page: “Offering to play a game with Alice when talking to her in the backyard” (up icon) (GAME, +1) and “Asking Alice about the garden when talking to her in the backyard” (up icon) (BACKYARD, +1). WEATHER and SCHOOL change nothing (the transcript shows no icon). The wiki says only that {{Alice}} is silent throughout the chapter, so the replies to WEATHER and SCHOOL are that she does not answer. Options that are buttons in the game show the game’s label first (GAME, BACKYARD, WEATHER, SCHOOL), then a short description; the spoken line is the game’s, quoted in the outcome.

nodes.title: Still in the backyard
nodes.whenNot: Kara did not stop to talk to Alice in the backyard.
nodes.situation: You are {{Kara}}, still in the backyard with {{Alice}}. You can say one more thing.

options.text: GAME: offer to play a game with her.
options.outcome: “You look bored. Would you like to play a game?” {{Alice}} briefly looks at {{Kara}}, then gets up and goes back inside.

options.text: BACKYARD: ask whether she likes playing out here.
options.outcome: “You like playing out here?” {{Alice}} glances at {{Kara}}, then gets up and goes back inside.

options.text: WEATHER: say it is not very nice out, and offer to get her a sweater.
options.outcome: “It’s not very nice out. You might catch cold. I could get you a sweater if you want.” {{Alice}} does not answer. She gets up and goes back inside.

options.text: SCHOOL: ask whether she is going to school today.
options.outcome: “Aren’t you going to school today?” {{Alice}} does not answer. She gets up and goes back inside.

nodes.adaptationNote: The second backyard menu (the transcript: “These are optional twice”): the same four lines minus the one already said. Same relationship changes as the first menu (GAME and BACKYARD +1 each; WEATHER and SCHOOL none), so the most the backyard gives is +2. Then {{Alice}} goes back inside (transcript) and the first floor continues. Options that are buttons in the game show the game’s label first (the same four), then a short description; the spoken line is the game’s, quoted in the outcome.

nodes.title: Going upstairs
nodes.situation: You are {{Kara}}. You climb the stairs, past toys left on the steps, into the upstairs hallway. Your urgent tasks up here: tidy {{Todd}}’s room and tidy {{Alice}}’s room. Optional: clean the bathroom and the restroom.
facts: Upstairs, your urgent tasks are {{Todd}}’s room and {{Alice}}’s room; the bathroom and the restroom are optional.

outcomes.0: {{Kara}} starts on the second floor.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s checkpoint GO UPSTAIRS, narrated as an event. The objectives are the transcript’s (urgent: TIDY TODD’S ROOM, TIDY ALICE’S ROOM; optional: CLEAN BATHROOM, CLEAN RESTROOM); the toys on the stairs are from the wiki’s Attention to Detail. No stat change.

nodes.title: The second floor
nodes.situation: You are {{Kara}}, upstairs in {{Todd}}’s house. Off the hallway are {{Todd}}’s bedroom, {{Alice}}’s room, a bathroom and a separate restroom, whose door is shut with {{Todd}} inside. Both bedrooms must be tidied; the bathroom and the restroom are optional. You can do one thing at a time, in any order. When both bedrooms are done you can talk to {{Alice}}.

options.text: Tidy {{Todd}}’s room: make the bed, clear the mess and open the window to air it.
options.fact: {{Todd}}’s bedroom was a mess of newspapers, bottles, chips, records and a guitar; an advertisement for a child android model fell out from among his bills. When you came out, {{Todd}} left the restroom and shoved you: “Watch it!”
options.outcome: {{Kara}} makes {{Todd}}’s bed; while she works, {{Alice}} walks past to her room. {{Kara}} moves the guitar off the floor, stacks the newspapers, clears the bottles and the leftover chips and puts the records back in their box. When she picks up the bills on the cabinet an advertisement for a child android model slips out; she looks at it and puts it back. She opens the window to air the room. A bottle of pills stands on the nightstand by the bed. As she steps back into the hallway, {{Todd}} comes out of the restroom and shoves her: “Watch it!”

options.text: Put away the pill bottle on {{Todd}}’s nightstand.
options.fact: {{Todd}} takes antidepressants (your scan: tianeptine, risk of behavioral disorders), and he keeps a handgun in the drawer of his nightstand.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} picks up the bottle and scans it: ANTIDEPRESSANT. Contains tianeptine. Risk of behavioral disorders. She opens the nightstand drawer to put it away. Inside lies a handgun. She closes the drawer.

options.text: Clean the toilet in the restroom.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} scrubs the toilet and closes the restroom door behind her.

options.text: Clean the bathroom: arrange the bottles, put the dirty clothes in the basket and mop the floor.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} lines up the body-wash bottles, gathers the dirty clothes off the floor into the basket and mops until the floor shines.

options.text: Tidy {{Alice}}’s room: make her bed.
options.fact: {{Alice}}’s room has a small tent in the corner, drawings on the walls, a shelf of books, a book on the floor, and a small box on the chest of drawers by the door.
options.outcome: {{Alice}}’s room: a small tent in the corner, drawings on the walls, a shelf of books, a book on the floor, a small box on the chest of drawers by the door. {{Kara}} pulls the blanket straight and fixes the pillow.

options.text: Tidy {{Alice}}’s room: make her bed.
options.fact: {{Alice}}’s room has a small tent in the corner, drawings on the walls, a shelf of books, a book on the floor, and a small box on the chest of drawers by the door.
options.outcome: As {{Kara}} comes in, {{Alice}} crawls into the small tent in the corner. “I just want to tidy up your room a little. I only need two minutes. Is that okay, {{Alice}}?” {{Alice}} watches her pull the blanket straight and fix the pillow. The room has drawings on the walls, a shelf of books, a book on the floor and a small box on the chest of drawers by the door.

options.text: Open {{Alice}}’s window to air the room.
options.fact: Below {{Alice}}’s bedroom window runs the edge of a roof: a way down from the second floor.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} pushes up the window and leans out. Below it runs the edge of a roof, a way down from the second floor. She goes back inside.

options.text: Look at the book on {{Alice}}’s floor.
options.fact: {{Alice}} has a copy of “{{Alice}} in Wonderland”.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} kneels and reads the cover: “{{Alice}} in Wonderland”. She gets back up without a word.

options.text: Look at the book on {{Alice}}’s floor.
options.fact: {{Alice}} has a copy of “{{Alice}} in Wonderland”; she smiled when you noticed it.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} kneels and reads the cover: “{{Alice}} in Wonderland…” She looks at {{Alice}} and smiles. “Of course.” {{Alice}} smiles back.

options.text: Pick up the small box on {{Alice}}’s chest of drawers.
options.fact: {{Alice}} keeps a small locked box on the chest of drawers by her door.
options.outcome: The box is locked. {{Kara}} shakes it gently, tries the lid and puts it back.

options.text: Kneel down and talk to {{Alice}}.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} kneels down to {{Alice}}’s level by the tent.

situationWhen.text: {{Alice}} is still downstairs.
{{Alice}} has come up to her room and sits in the little tent in the corner with her toy fox.

nodes.title: {{Todd}}’s bedroom: a magazine and the TV
nodes.situation: You are {{Kara}}, back in the upstairs hallway; the rooms are done. {{Todd}}’s bedroom door is open. A magazine lies on the cupboard by the door, and the small TV in the room can be switched on.

media.title: All Sports: Android QB
facts: All Sports reports that {{CyberLife}} has unveiled a “technical demo” android quarterback that can throw from end zone to end zone, hit a target six inches wide and run over 1,500 plays. American football has so far stayed human; the founder of an anti-android fan group says {{CyberLife}} hopes “to distort our sport the same way they have all the others.”

media.title: Tech Addict: The Price of Life
facts: Tech Addict explains how driverless cars choose whom to hit: the car’s imaging reads a pedestrian’s age, gender and life expectancy, public records add marital status, employment record and whether they have children, and each possible victim gets a “value”, with “a premium on lives that will save other lives, like doctors and nurses.” A critic answers that a criminal record does not make anyone less valuable: “That kind of information is irrelevant to the sanctity of human life.”

media.title: the TV in {{Todd}}’s bedroom
facts: On the sports news, the league is negotiating whether to allow one android player per basketball squad, and {{CyberLife}} has offered one specialized model to every team; androids already train players and advise coaches, but none has been allowed to compete.
The news: another 225,000 jobs were lost from the US economy in October, bringing unemployment up to 37.3%.

The news: President {{Warren}} opened a new {{CyberLife}} plant near Milwaukee, praised {{CyberLife}}’s role in the economy, and announced that the Department of Defense will acquire 200,000 android combat units.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s two optional nodes READ “ANDROID QB” and READ “PUTTING A PRICE” (the chart’s label for the article “The Price of Life”): one magazine on the cupboard by the door of {{Todd}}’s room, with two covers. With them, the bedroom TV, which is not a chart node: Channel 16 sports, an animated film, CTN’s job figures, a hockey game and KNC on the President; the film and the hockey are left out. In the game both are available while cleaning his room and again after the talk with {{Alice}} (the transcript’s “Back In Hallway”); here they come after the talk. Facts are summarized from the transcript; presenters and interviewees are not named. No public-opinion effect (the Public Opinion page lists nothing for this chapter). Dropped from the earlier R04: the stock market “up 11 percent” and “New Orleans may be underwater by 2055”, for which no source in this chapter exists.

nodes.title: Finished cleaning
nodes.situation: You are {{Kara}}. Your chores are done, and you go back downstairs. {{Alice}} sits at the dining table playing with her toy fox. {{Todd}}: “What are you doing?” {{Alice}}, nervously: “I… I’m playing…” “You’re playing…” He walks around the table. “I know what you’re thinking… You think your dad’s a lowlife… Huh? Fuckin’ loser? Can’t get a job, take care of his family? Don’t you think I tried to make things work!? But whatever I do when someone comes along, they just FUCK IT ALL UP!” He throws a chair aside. “I know what you think of me… You hate me… You hate me don’t ya?” He kicks a chair and grabs {{Alice}}. “SAY IT! YOU HATE ME!” {{Alice}} cries. He puts her down. “God… What am I doing? I’m sorry, honey, I’m sorry…” He hugs her, crying. “You know I love you, don’t you? You know I love you…” Over his shoulder, {{Alice}} looks at you.

The dirty dishes and the magazine are still on the table where she sits.

facts: {{Todd}} raged at {{Alice}} at the dining table, threw a chair, grabbed her and shouted “SAY IT! YOU HATE ME!”, then broke down, apologized and hugged her: “You know I love you, don’t you?”

nodes.title: The magazine in the living room

media.title: Century: The North Pole - Why Russia Wants It
facts: Century (cover: “Frozen treasures”; also “Is President {{Warren}} too close to {{CyberLife}}?”) reports that Russia’s interest in the North Pole has intensified since precious minerals used in synthesizing thirium were found trapped in the ice; surplus reserves would let either the US or Russia build more advanced androids and greatly boost its military and industrial output. NATO says “A conflict would benefit nobody”; President {{Warren}}: “It’s simple. Russia has no business in the Arctic. If the Kremlin doesn’t understand that, we will make them understand.”

media.title: {{Detroit}} Today: Life Found on Titan!
facts: {{Detroit}} Today (cover: “Life Found on Titan!”; also “NATO Security Council divided over Arctic dispute”) reports that a probe launched nineteen years ago has confirmed microorganisms living hundreds of kilometers below Titan’s surface, in a salt-water ocean under thick ice; after similar finds on Enceladus, life may be common in the universe. NASA calls its android expedition to Io one of many voyages seeking extraterrestrial life, and {{CyberLife}} says its space-faring androids are specially designed for long-range missions of this kind.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s optional side nodes READ “NORTH POLE RUSSIA” and READ “LIFE ON TITAN”: one magazine on the living-room table in front of the TV with two covers (the transcript’s “Read Magazine” with two tabs; BOOKWORM No. 2 and No. 27), drawn on the chart with no line to the main path. nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s CRIME SCENE bracket as a repeatable scene: each visit offers what has not been examined yet, one thing at a time; the scene keeps one opaque ID across visits. Every chart node in the bracket is an option, after the report to {{Hank}} (offered only once the investigation is complete), in the order of the police markers, then the bathroom (whose statue is the tenth evidence item; story 1.9.2 moved it up from among the other looks), and then the rest: ANALYZE CARLOS’ BODY (the template’s Body clues), RECONSTRUCT CARLOS’ LAST MOMENTS (needs the body), ANALYZE KNIFE (2), ANALYZE RED ICE (3), the blood at marker 4 (PowerPyx; no chart node of its own), ANALYZE BLOOD ON WALLS (two options, markers 5 and 6, as PowerPyx counts them), EXAMINE CHAIR (7), ANALYZE MISSING KNIFE (8), ANALYZE BASEBALL BAT (9; the template’s Bat clue), RECONSTRUCT ASSAULT WITH BAT (needs the bat), EXAMINE EDEN CLUB FLYER, ANALYZE BACKYARD (the template’s Prints clue; the shoe print reads K52 as in the template), INVESTIGATE WRITING, SAMPLE BLOOD (the template’s Blood clue; in the game any blood can be tasted once), OPEN CLOSET, CHECK SHOWER (chart state CONNOR KNOWS ABOUT RA9), EXAMINE STATUE (needs the shower; chart state CONNOR HAVE SEEN THE STATUE), READ “ANDROID SEX” and READ “ANDROID SPY” (the two magazines are options here, not a separate media scene, because in the game they lie in the kitchen and cost investigation time). Evidence: the investigation is complete (CONNOR KNOWS WHAT HAPPENED, the transcript’s REVIEW EVIDENCE 10/10) once all ten evidence items are reviewed. The wiki transcript prints the REVIEW EVIDENCE n/10 counter under exactly ten interactions: the victim’s reconstruction, the knife, the red ice, the blood at markers 4, 5 and 6, the bathroom (counted once, after the statue, as in its tab), the chair, the missing knife and the bat reconstruction; Read Flyer and Check Backyard have no counter, so they are not evidence (story 1.9.1 counted them, from PowerPyx’s list of eleven, and did not count the bathroom). The statue therefore cannot be missed on a FOUND DEVIANT run. The fastest complete search is thirteen actions (the ten items plus the body scan, the bat scan and the shower that unlock three of them). Then the option to report to {{Hank}} appears; the other looks stay open. Timer (unsourced as a count): the game’s “approximately five minutes” is modelled as 13 actions. If the 13th action leaves the investigation incomplete, {{Hank}} wants to go (the next scenes); if he grants five more minutes, those are 5 further actions, after which he leaves (OUT OF TIME). Once {{Connor}} knows what happened the clock stops (the transcript’s two branches are “Know What Happened” or “Run Out Of Time”). {{Hank}}’s idle moves are the only cue the game gives, so they appear as the clock runs: after 7 actions he opens the closet, tosses the flyer, comments on the red ice and a technician mentions the bathroom; after 10 he wanders the kitchen and eyes the door. {{Hank}}’s reactions to the blood sample (shown only if he is watching, in the game) and to the backyard are part of those outcomes. Each look adds a short fact to {{Connor}}’s knowledge (the four blood looks share one); the full scan text is in the outcome. Left out, no effect and not on the chart: the windows and the curtain that drops the brooms. No stat change in the search itself. Cross-chapter outputs: ch06SawWriting, ch06KnowsRA9, ch06SawStatue (and evidence.statueMap, read by the archive route in Last Chance, {{Connor}}), and ch06Clues for everything examined, including the magazines.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s CONNOR KNOWS WHAT HAPPENED and REPORT TO LT. ANDERSON, then the choice RECONSTRUCT THE CRIME (check) or FAIL TO RECONSTRUCT THE CRIME (cross), as one repeatable scene with one opaque ID: the template’s five prompts, asked in order, each with the game’s three button labels; the module rotates their display order deterministically by question and remaps IDs to positions (correct positions 1, 3, 2, 1, 3), a deliberate departure from the template order to remove the always-first answer cue. A wrong answer repeats the question (PowerPyx: “If you choose incorrectly, you will answer until you pick the bat”) with {{Hank}}’s “No, that can’t be right… It doesn’t fit the evidence.”, then “Your story makes no sense… You’ve gotta stick to the facts.”; the third mistake in all ends it (template note: “After three mistakes, he will leave.”), with the template’s Hank small down (−1) and FAIL TO RECONSTRUCT THE CRIME. The first question is not a mistake: {{Hank}} points to the kitchen and the report goes on (transcript and PowerPyx: “Regardless of what you choose, Connor and Hank will move to the kitchen”). Five correct answers: RECONSTRUCT THE CRIME, with one Hank small up in total, on the thirium explanation (+1 when {{Hank}} is impressed; operator, 2026-11-07, two replays, level read in the chart header): both replays showed a single small up across the reconstruction and the explanation, on the blue-blood line, taking Hank from HOSTILE to TENSE in Run A and leaving him NEUTRAL in Run B, where a second small up would have read WARM. The template and the wiki chapter page also give the correct reconstruction its own small up; it was not seen on screen and is not applied (the two sources may list one arrow twice). Story 1.9.2 and earlier applied both; this scene’s reconstructionArrows: 1 (story 1.9.3) selects the single arrow, and older story snapshots, which lack it, replay with two. The chapter page’s separate “Failing to solve the crime” down is not added on top.

nodes.title: Breaking the order
nodes.situation: You are {{Kara}}. It is a stormy night, a little after nine. You have made dinner with what little was in the kitchen. {{Todd}} has been asleep on the couch; {{Alice}} sits at the dining table, watching the rain on the street. You wake him: “{{Todd}}?” “Huh?!” “Dinner is ready.” “Yeah, yeah, I’m coming…” You turn on the light over the table and serve: “There wasn’t much in the kitchen, I did what I could.” {{Todd}}, high on red ice, talks at nobody: “Life’s funny… I lost my job cause of androids… then when I need somebody to take care of this goddamn house, what do I do? I go out and hire a fucking android… What a joke!” You stand by the table and wait on them. Then he turns on {{Alice}}: “What are you looking at?... What’s your fuckin’ problem? Not the life you dreamed of, eh? … Maybe you think it’s my fault we live in this fuckin’ shithole, my fault your fuckin’ mother took off? … It’s all your fault!” He throws the table aside and hits her. “Daddy, no…” She runs upstairs. “It’s all your fucking fault! Get back here! Come back here right now!” He turns to you: “It’s all her fault... I gotta teach her a good fucking lesson… First, I need a little hit… You stay there! Don’t you dare fucking move, or I’ll bust you worse than last time.” On the couch he smokes and talks to himself: “Whore took off, without a word… I could’ve been happy… I coulda had a family… It’s all her fault… Yeah... I gotta teach her some respect!” He has his belt in his hand. “{{Alice}}! Daddy’s very mad! You deserve to be taught a good lesson… A good fuckin’ lesson…” His order stands in front of you like a wall: DON’T MOVE. Your programming does not let you cross it.

options.text: BREAK PROGRAMMING: push through the wall of the order and move.
options.fact: You broke through {{Todd}}’s order not to move. Your programming could not hold you.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} pushes against the wall of the order. It cracks, and shatters. She can move.

options.text: Stay where he told you to stand.
options.outcome: {{Kara}} does not move. {{Todd}} goes up the stairs. “{{Alice}}! You and I have a little score to settle. Come on, come here you little brat!” “No, Daddy, no! Don’t hurt me! Please, don’t hurt me!” “Come outta there! Don’t make me come and get you! It’s all your fault! It’s all your fault! She left because of you! Stop wriggling! I’ll teach you to respect your father! … I’m gonna give you a thrashin’ you won’t forget in a hurry.” Then the screaming stops. When {{Kara}} goes up, {{Alice}} lies still on the floor of her room and {{Todd}} is crouched beside her: “It’s all over now… Daddy isn’t angry anymore… Daddy loves you. You know Daddy loves you…” He sees {{Kara}}. “This is your fault. This is all your fault. None of this woulda happened if it weren’t for you. THIS IS ALL YOUR FAULT!” He turns on her and destroys her.

nodes.adaptationNote: The chart’s opening checkpoints DINNER’S READY and TODD GETS MAD and the arrow WAIT ON TODD & ALICE (PowerPyx: “Unmissable”) are narrated in the situation, followed by the order “Don’t move” and the choice the chart draws as BREAK PROGRAMMING → KARA BECOMES DEVIANT or KARA FAILS TO BECOME DEVIANT → TODD KILLS ALICE (ending, not-required icon; {{Kara}} is destroyed too, per the Kara page: “Todd blaming Kara despite clearly doing so and destroying her”). Lines are the game’s text (template “In Todd’s House”, “Turned on the light”, “Walking around after serving”, “IF Don’t move”, “Todd in the living room”, “IF Don’t go / Don’t become a deviant”). In the game the dinner is free roam with dialogue variants and no prompt: serving at once or late, turning on the light or being told to (“Turn on the lights! Can’t see shit.”), and moving while {{Todd}} rants (“Stop moving around for Chrissake!”). The template has no choice group there and nothing depends on it, so the narration takes the plain path (light on, served, standing still). Not offered for a second reason: the shared regression test “a dead protagonist never receives future decisions” allows only K02 as a chapter-7 scene before the wall. The napkin on {{Alice}}’s lap (wiki Notes) is left out. The wall is BREAK PROGRAMMING, a held input with no failure branch on the chart, so it carries no risk. No stat change: the template has no arrow in this chapter.

Don’t hurt me! Please, don’t hurt me!” “Come outta there! Don’t make me come and get you! It’s all your fault! It’s all your fault! She left because of you! Stop wriggling! I’ll teach you to respect your father! … I’m gonna give you a thrashin’ you won’t forget in a hurry.” Then the screaming stops. When {{Kara}} goes up, {{Alice}} lies still on the floor of her room and {{Todd}} is crouched beside her: “It’s all over now… Daddy isn’t angry anymore… Daddy loves you. You know Daddy loves you…” He sees {{Kara}}. “This is your fault. This is all your fault. None of this woulda happened if it weren’t for you. In free roam the chart offers four ways on: GO UPSTAIRS; REASON WITH TODD (→ K03r); standing in his path, KARA IS IN TODD’S WAY DOWNSTAIRS → TODD SHOVES KARA DOWNSTAIRS → TODD GOES UPSTAIRS (→ GET TO ALICE AFTER TODD, with TAKE GUN offered first if the gun was seen in A New Home); and doing nothing, KARA IS TOO SLOW → TODD KILLS ALICE (PowerPyx: “Walk to the kitchen instead and do nothing until the final cutscene starts”). Also from the wiki: becoming free only as {{Todd}} heads upstairs removes REASON WITH TODD; the benchmark always offers it. No stat change.

The template’s prompt in the game’s order: RUN WITH ALICE (chart RUN AWAY), LOCK ROOM (chart LOCK DOOR; PowerPyx: “a time window of 10 seconds”), SPEAK TO TODD (chart REASON WITH TODD → TODD SHOVES KARA UPSTAIRS → GET TO ALICE AFTER TODD), and the timeout default [ OUT OF TIME ] (chart TODD IS COMING → OUT OF TIME → TODD BREAKS INTO BEDROOM). She’s mine. I do what I want with her.” He knocks {{Kara}} down and drags {{Alice}} into her room. “No, Dad! NO!”

nodes.adaptationNote: After RUN WITH ALICE, the chart’s check FAIL TO HIDE (✗) / HIDE IN CORRIDOR (✓). PowerPyx: hide “in either room with holding Square or O. When he walks past, let go off the button and proceed to the stairs”; to fail, “Go out of Alice’s room and don’t move any further, until Todd comes”. So staying is a choice, and hiding is a held input that can fail: a 10% risk, which no source gives (the benchmark’s value). Failing leads, with the template’s lines, to TODD TAKES ALICE TO HER ROOM → GET TO ALICE AFTER TODD (TAKE GUN first if the gun was seen); hiding leads to TODD REALIZES KARA AND ALICE ARE GONE (K04r).
